claim: Sleep depriving mice affects clock-gene expression.
source: Sleep depriving mice affects clock-gene expression, suggesting that these genes contribute to sleep homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that motivates the study.

claim: Clock genes contribute to sleep homeostasis.
source: Sleep depriving mice affects clock-gene expression, suggesting that these genes contribute to sleep homeostasis.
evidence: The abstract states this as a suggested relationship based on prior observations.

claim: CIRBP's rhythmic expression is sleep-wake driven.
source: We propose CIRBP to play a role because its rhythmic expression is i) sleep-wake driven and ii) necessary for high-amplitude clock-gene expression in vitro.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a property of CIRBP.

claim: CIRBP is necessary for high-amplitude clock-gene expression in vitro.
source: We propose CIRBP to play a role because its rhythmic expression is i) sleep-wake driven and ii) necessary for high-amplitude clock-gene expression in vitro.
evidence: The abstract cites in vitro findings about CIRBP's role.

claim: Lack of CIRBP blunted the sleep-deprivation incurred changes in cortical expression of Nr1d1.
source: Lack of CIRBP indeed blunted the sleep-deprivation incurred changes in cortical expression of Nr1d1, whereas it amplified the changes in Per2 and Clock.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Lack of CIRBP amplified the sleep-deprivation incurred changes in cortical expression of Per2.
source: Lack of CIRBP indeed blunted the sleep-deprivation incurred changes in cortical expression of Nr1d1, whereas it amplified the changes in Per2 and Clock.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Lack of CIRBP amplified the sleep-deprivation incurred changes in cortical expression of Clock.
source: Lack of CIRBP indeed blunted the sleep-deprivation incurred changes in cortical expression of Nr1d1, whereas it amplified the changes in Per2 and Clock.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Cirbp KO mice accrued only half the extra REM sleep wild-type littermates obtained during recovery.
source: Concerning sleep homeostasis, KO mice accrued only half the extra REM sleep wild-type (WT) littermates obtained during recovery.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Cirbp KO mice were more active during lights-off compared to WT mice.
source: Unexpectedly, KO mice were more active during lights-off which was accompanied with faster theta oscillations compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is an unexpected finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Cirbp KO mice had faster theta oscillations during lights-off compared to WT mice.
source: Unexpectedly, KO mice were more active during lights-off which was accompanied with faster theta oscillations compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is an unexpected finding reported in the abstract.

claim: CIRBP adjusts cortical clock-gene expression after sleep deprivation.
source: Thus, CIRBP adjusts cortical clock-gene expression after sleep deprivation and expedites REM-sleep recovery.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: CIRBP expedites REM-sleep recovery.
source: Thus, CIRBP adjusts cortical clock-gene expression after sleep deprivation and expedites REM-sleep recovery.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: The sleep-wake distribution is coordinated by the interaction of a circadian and a sleep homeostatic process.
source: The sleep-wake distribution is coordinated by the interaction of a circadian and a sleep homeostatic process (Daan et al., 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: CLOCK/NPAS2:BMAL1 heterodimers drive the transcription of Period, Cryptochrome and Rev-Erb genes.
source: CLOCK/NPAS2:BMAL1 (ARNTL) heterodimers drive the transcription of many target genes, among them the Period (Per1-2), Cryptochome (Cry1, −2) and Rev-Erb (Nr1d1, −2) genes.
evidence: This describes the molecular basis of the circadian clock.

claim: PER:CRY complexes inhibit CLOCK/NPAS2:ARNTL-transcriptional activity.
source: Subsequently, PER:CRY complexes inhibit CLOCK/NPAS2:ARNTL-transcriptional activity thereby preventing their own transcription.
evidence: This describes a feedback mechanism in the circadian clock.

claim: NR1D1 regulates the transcription of Arntl.
source: In addition, clock components such as the transcriptional repressor NR1D1 regulate the transcription of Arntl, ensuring together with other transcriptional feedback loops a period of ca. 24 hr (Lowrey and Takahashi, 2011).
evidence: This describes the role of NR1D1 in the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: Clock-gene circuitry ensures a period of approximately 24 hours.
source: In addition, clock components such as the transcriptional repressor NR1D1 regulate the transcription of Arntl, ensuring together with other transcriptional feedback loops a period of ca. 24 hr (Lowrey and Takahashi, 2011).
evidence: This is a fundamental property of the circadian clock.

claim: Peripherally generated circadian rhythms are coordinated by a central pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nuclei.
source: While this clock-gene circuitry is functionally expressed in almost each cell of the body, peripherally generated circadian rhythms are coordinated by a central pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) of the hypothalamus, assuring proper circadian time-keeping at the organismal level (Hastings et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the hierarchical organization of circadian clocks.

claim: The sleep homeostatic process keeps track of time spent awake and asleep.
source: The sleep homeostatic process keeps track of time spent awake and asleep, during which sleep pressure is increasing and decreasing.
evidence: This is a definition of the sleep homeostatic process.

claim: The mechanisms and specific brain structure(s) underlying the sleep homeostatic process are to date unknown.
source: The mechanisms and specific brain structure(s) underlying this process are to date unknown.
evidence: This states the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Mutations in circadian clock genes are associated with an altered sleep homeostatic response to sleep deprivation in mice, fruit flies and humans.
source: This is supported by studies in several species (i.e. mice, fruit flies and humans), showing that mutations in circadian clock genes are associated with an altered sleep homeostatic response to sleep deprivation (e.g. Mang et al., 2016; Shaw et al., 2002; Viola et al., 2007; Wisor et al., 2002; He et al., 2009).
evidence: This summarizes findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Disrupting circadian rhythms in the tuberomammillary nucleus through removal of Arntl affects the regulation of time spent in NREM sleep after sleep deprivation.
source: Disrupting circadian rhythms in the tuberomammillary nucleus, however, through removal of the core clock gene Arntl, affects the regulation of time spent in NREM sleep after sleep deprivation, implying that specific nuclei can impact aspects of the sleep homeostatic process (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites a specific study showing regional effects on sleep homeostasis.

claim: Enforced wakefulness affects the expression of clock genes Nr1d1, Per1-3 and Dbp in the brain.
source: An additional argument for a role for clock genes in sleep homeostasis comes from studies showing that enforced wakefulness affects the expression of clock genes, such as Nr1d1, Per1-3 and Dbp, in the brain (Mongrain et al., 2010).
evidence: This cites evidence linking sleep deprivation to clock gene expression changes.

claim: Sleep-deprivation induced changes in clock-gene expression were most pronounced in the cerebral cortex.
source: These sleep-deprivation induced changes in clock-gene expression were most pronounced in the cerebral cortex, while expression in the SCN remained unperturbed (Curie et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites a study showing regional differences in clock gene responses to sleep deprivation.

claim: Clock-gene expression in the SCN remained unperturbed by sleep deprivation.
source: These sleep-deprivation induced changes in clock-gene expression were most pronounced in the cerebral cortex, while expression in the SCN remained unperturbed (Curie et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites a study showing the SCN is resistant to sleep deprivation effects.

claim: Decreasing temperature in vitro increases CIRBP levels.
source: Decreasing temperature in vitro increase CIRBP levels (Nishiyama et al., 1997) and daily changes in mice core body temperature are sufficient to drive robust cyclic levels of Cirbp and CIRBP (Morf et al., 2012) in anti-phase with temperature.
evidence: This cites in vitro evidence for temperature regulation of CIRBP.

claim: Daily changes in mice core body temperature are sufficient to drive robust cyclic levels of Cirbp and CIRBP in anti-phase with temperature.
source: Decreasing temperature in vitro increase CIRBP levels (Nishiyama et al., 1997) and daily changes in mice core body temperature are sufficient to drive robust cyclic levels of Cirbp and CIRBP (Morf et al., 2012) in anti-phase with temperature.
evidence: This cites evidence for temperature-driven CIRBP rhythms in vivo.

claim: More than 80% of the variance in daily changes in cortical temperature in rats is explained by the sleep-wake distribution.
source: Although daily changes in cortical temperature appear circadian, in the rat more than 80% of its variance is explained by the sleep-wake distribution (Franken et al., 1992).
evidence: This cites a quantitative finding from a previous study in rats.

claim: When controlling for daily sleep-wake driven changes in cortical temperature by sleep deprivations, the daily rhythms of cortical Cirbp become strongly attenuated.
source: Hence, when controlling for the daily sleep-wake driven changes in cortical temperature by sleep deprivations, the daily rhythms of cortical Cirbp become strongly attenuated (see Figure 1, based on Gene Expression Omnibus number GSE9442 from Maret et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1 from a previous study.

claim: Cirbp shows the highest down-regulation of all genes after sleep deprivation.
source: Furthermore, the expression of the gene Cirbp shows the highest down-regulation of all genes after sleep deprivation (Mongrain et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010), underscoring its sleep-wake-dependent expression.
evidence: This cites studies showing Cirbp is highly responsive to sleep deprivation.

claim: Temperature-driven changes in CIRBP are required for high amplitude clock-gene expression in temperature-synchronized cells.
source: Two independent studies have shown that the temperature-driven changes in CIRBP are required for high amplitude clock-gene expression in temperature-synchronized cells (Morf et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This cites two independent in vitro studies.

claim: The sleep-wake distribution in the mouse is the major determinant of cortical temperature changes.
source: Our results demonstrate that like in the rat, the sleep-wake distribution in the mouse is the major determinant of cortical temperature changes, with a significant, albeit small, contribution of locomotor activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the Discussion.

claim: Locomotor activity makes a significant, albeit small, contribution to cortical temperature changes in mice.
source: Our results demonstrate that like in the rat, the sleep-wake distribution in the mouse is the major determinant of cortical temperature changes, with a significant, albeit small, contribution of locomotor activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the Discussion.

claim: Lack of CIRBP attenuated the sleep-deprivation-induced changes in the cortical expression of Nr1d1.
source: In line with our predictions, we found that a lack of CIRBP attenuated the sleep-deprivation-induced changes in the cortical expression of Nr1d1 and the homeostatic response in REM-sleep time.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: Lack of CIRBP attenuated the homeostatic response in REM-sleep time.
source: In line with our predictions, we found that a lack of CIRBP attenuated the sleep-deprivation-induced changes in the cortical expression of Nr1d1 and the homeostatic response in REM-sleep time.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: Differences in Per2 and Clock expression after sleep deprivation were augmented in Cirbp KO mice.
source: However, in contrast to our hypothesis, we observed that differences in Per2 and Clock expression after sleep deprivation were augmented in Cirbp KO mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Discussion that contradicts the hypothesis.

claim: Cirbp KO mice were substantially more active during the dark phase of the 24 hr period when compared to their WT littermates.
source: Unexpectedly, these mice were also substantially more active during the dark phase of the 24 hr period when compared to their WT littermates, without increasing their time spent awake.
evidence: This is an unexpected finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: Cirbp KO mice did not increase their time spent awake despite being more active during the dark phase.
source: Unexpectedly, these mice were also substantially more active during the dark phase of the 24 hr period when compared to their WT littermates, without increasing their time spent awake.
evidence: This is an unexpected finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: The increase in locomotor activity in Cirbp KO mice was accompanied by an acceleration of EEG theta oscillations during active waking.
source: This increase in locomotor activity was accompanied by an acceleration of electroencephalogram (EEG) theta oscillations during active waking.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: Cirbp contributes to some of the sleep-deprivation-induced changes in clock-gene expression.
source: Altogether, our data show that Cirbp contributes to some of the sleep-deprivation-induced changes in clock-gene expression, but also points to the existence of other sleep-wake-driven pathways transferring sleep-wake state information to clock-gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: Other sleep-wake-driven pathways besides CIRBP transfer sleep-wake state information to clock-gene expression.
source: Altogether, our data show that Cirbp contributes to some of the sleep-deprivation-induced changes in clock-gene expression, but also points to the existence of other sleep-wake-driven pathways transferring sleep-wake state information to clock-gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete effect of CIRBP knockout.

claim: Fast changes in cortical temperature occur at sleep-wake state transitions.
source: Closer inspection of cortical temperature changes revealed rapid fluctuations associated with sleep-wake state transitions.
evidence: This is a finding from the Results section.

claim: When entering NREM sleep, cortical temperature consistently decreased.
source: When entering NREM sleep, cortical temperature consistently decreased, whereas at transitions into wake and REM sleep, it increased.
evidence: This is a specific finding about temperature changes at sleep transitions.

claim: At transitions into wake and REM sleep, cortical temperature increased.
source: When entering NREM sleep, cortical temperature consistently decreased, whereas at transitions into wake and REM sleep, it increased.
evidence: This is a specific finding about temperature changes at sleep transitions.

claim: Within 1.5 min of transitioning from NREM to REM sleep, an increase of 0.4°C in cortical temperature was observed.
source: This latter transition was characterized by a fast and consistent change in cortical temperature, where within 1.5 min an increase of 0.4°C was observed.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the magnitude and speed of temperature change.

claim: Transitions from REM sleep into wake led to an initial decrease in cortical temperature.
source: Transitions from REM sleep into wake led to an initial decrease in cortical temperature, contrasting with the increase observed in the wakefulness when following NREM sleep.
evidence: This is a specific finding about temperature dynamics at REM-to-wake transitions.

claim: Both waking and locomotor activity strongly correlated with cortical temperature.
source: Importantly, the time course of cortical temperature was strongly correlated to both waking (Figure 3-B left: WT: R2 = 0.76; KO: R2 = 0.81, p<0.0001) and locomotor activity (Figure 3-B right: WT: R2 = 0.60; KO: R2 = 0.72, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support shown in Figure 3-B.

claim: Cortical temperature during sleep deprivation did not differ from levels reached after long waking bouts during baseline.
source: Cortical temperature reached in these bouts did not differ during sleep deprivation and spontaneous wakefulness in WT mice (Figure 3-C), nor in KO mice (t(5)=0.84, p=0.44), indicating that factors other than extended wakefulness (e.g. light exposure, circadian time, sleep deprivation-associated stress) do not expressly contribute to these changes.
evidence: This finding rules out stress as a major contributor to temperature changes during sleep deprivation.

claim: Waking is the major determinant of cortical temperature after correcting for locomotor activity.
source: Waking after correcting for LMA is the major determinant of Tcx, as revealed by partial correlation analysis; here performed on the combined hourly values of all WT mice.
evidence: This is shown by partial correlation analysis in Figure 3-D.

claim: A 6 hr sleep deprivation caused a decrease in cortical and hepatic Cirbp expression relative to levels in non-sleep deprived controls.
source: In contrast, a 6 hr sleep deprivation caused a decrease in cortical and hepatic Cirbp expression relative to levels in non-sleep deprived controls (cortex: Figure 4-A; liver: Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding shown in Figure 4-A and supplement.

claim: After sleep deprivation, Rbm3-short expression decreased in the cortex and liver.
source: In addition, we confirmed that after sleep deprivation Rbm3-short expression decreased in the cortex (Figure 4-A) and liver (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), whereas Rbm3-long increased in cortex.
evidence: This confirms previous findings about Rbm3 isoform responses to sleep deprivation.

claim: After sleep deprivation, Rbm3-long expression increased in cortex.
source: In addition, we confirmed that after sleep deprivation Rbm3-short expression decreased in the cortex (Figure 4-A) and liver (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), whereas Rbm3-long increased in cortex.
evidence: This confirms previous findings about Rbm3 isoform responses to sleep deprivation.

claim: Cortical expression of Homer1a, Dusp4, Hspa5, Hsp90b1 and Hsf1 was increased by sleep deprivation.
source: As anticipated, cortical expression of the waking-induced transcripts Homer1a, Dusp4, Hspa5, Hsp90b1 and Hsf1 was increased by sleep deprivation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This confirms expected responses of wake-induced genes to sleep deprivation.

claim: The effect of sleep deprivation on Hsp90b1 and Hspa5 transcripts was significantly amplified in Cirbp KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: Furthermore, the effect of sleep deprivation on the transcripts Hsp90b1 and Hspa5 was significantly amplified in Cirbp KO mice compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is a genotype-specific finding about heat shock protein responses.

claim: In the cortex of WT mice, sleep deprivation increased cortical Per2, decreased Dbp and Nr1d1 and did not significantly affect Clock and Npas2.
source: Indeed, in the cortex of WT mice, sleep deprivation increased cortical Per2, decreased Dbp and Nr1d1 and did not significantly affect Clock and Npas2 (Figure 4-C).
evidence: This confirms expected clock gene responses to sleep deprivation in WT mice.

claim: CIRBP attenuated the sleep-deprivation-induced changes of cortical Nr1d1.
source: Conform our hypothesis, CIRBP attenuated the sleep-deprivation-induced changes of cortical Nr1d1, a transcriptional repressor recently implicated in the sleep homeostat (Mang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding that supports the hypothesis.

claim: The effect of sleep deprivation on Per2 was amplified in Cirbp KO mice.
source: This observation contrasts with the genotype-dependent changes in Per2, because when considering the lower levels of cortical Per2 in Cirbp KO mice at ZT0, the effect of sleep deprivation was amplified in KO mice (Figure 4-C, two-way ANOVA, ZT0-ZT6[SD], interaction effect genotype x sleep deprivation: F(1,16)=12.4, p=0.003).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical support.

claim: The expression of Clock in the cortex was significantly increased by sleep deprivation in Cirbp KO mice and not in WT littermates.
source: Additionally, the expression of Clock in the cortex was significantly increased by sleep deprivation in Cirbp KO mice and not in WT littermates.
evidence: This is a genotype-specific finding about Clock gene response.

claim: Clock-gene expression in the liver appeared more resilient to the effects of sleep deprivation compared to the cortex.
source: Compared to the cortex, the clock-gene expression in the liver appeared more resilient to the effects of sleep deprivation, as only Dbp and Nr1d1 were significantly affected and not Per2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparative finding between tissues.

claim: During the 2 baseline days, no significant differences were observed in waking, NREM or REM sleep between Cirbp KO and WT mice.
source: During the 2 baseline days, no significant differences were observed in waking, NREM or REM sleep, both in terms of time spent during light and dark phases (Table 2), and in their distribution across the day (see Figure 5-A and Figure 6-A).
evidence: This establishes that baseline sleep is normal in KO mice.

claim: Under constant darkness, no change in circadian period length was detected between Cirbp KO and WT mice.
source: Of note, under constant darkness we did not detect any change in circadian period length (period [hours]: WT (n = 5): 23.8 ± 0.03 and KO (n = 7): 23.8 ± 0.01).
evidence: This shows that CIRBP does not affect the circadian clock period.

claim: At the end of the first recovery day, both KO and WT mice had gained ca. 40 min of NREM sleep relative to baseline.
source: At the end of the first recovery day, both KO and WT mice had gained ca. 40 min of NREM sleep relative to baseline (Figure 5-B, upper panel).
evidence: This shows that NREM sleep recovery is similar between genotypes.

claim: The increase in REM sleep during recovery was significantly attenuated by 46% in Cirbp KO mice.
source: At the end of recovery day 1, both WT and KO mice spent more time in REM sleep compared to corresponding baseline hours. However, this increase was significantly attenuated by 46% in Cirbp KO mice (Figure 5-B, lower panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding about REM sleep homeostasis.

claim: CIRBP did not affect the processes underlying NREM sleep intensity and NREM sleep time.
source: Thus, although CIRBP did not affect the processes underlying NREM sleep intensity and NREM sleep time, it did contribute to REM sleep homeostasis by increasing the amount of REM sleep after sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sleep homeostasis findings.

claim: CIRBP contributes to REM sleep homeostasis by increasing the amount of REM sleep after sleep deprivation.
source: Thus, although CIRBP did not affect the processes underlying NREM sleep intensity and NREM sleep time, it did contribute to REM sleep homeostasis by increasing the amount of REM sleep after sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the REM sleep recovery findings.

claim: Cirbp KO mice were more active than their WT littermates during the dark phase.
source: We observed that Cirbp KO mice were more active than their WT littermates during the dark phase (t(31)=-2.56, p=0.015, see also Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding with statistical support.

claim: Cirbp KO mice were almost twice as active in the 6 hr after dark onset compared to WT mice.
source: Specifically, Cirbp KO mice were almost twice as active in the 6 hr after dark onset (ZT12-18; movements: WT: 463.8 ± 60.7, KO: 801.8 ± 118.4, t(35)=-2.7, p=0.012; Figure 6-A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the magnitude of the activity difference.

claim: The increase in locomotor activity in Cirbp KO mice was not associated with a significant increase in time spent awake during baseline.
source: Interestingly, this increase was not associated with a significant increase in time spent awake during baseline (per 12 hr: t(35)=1.2, p=0.24, and see Table 2), and indeed Cirbp KO mice were more active per unit of waking (average in the dark phase, locomotor activity [movements/waking(min)], WT: 1.3 ± 0.13, KO: 2.1 ± 0.28; t(35)=-2.7, p=0.01).
evidence: This shows that increased activity is not due to more waking time.

claim: Cirbp KO mice were more active per unit of waking during the dark phase compared to WT mice.
source: Interestingly, this increase was not associated with a significant increase in time spent awake during baseline (per 12 hr: t(35)=1.2, p=0.24, and see Table 2), and indeed Cirbp KO mice were more active per unit of waking (average in the dark phase, locomotor activity [movements/waking(min)], WT: 1.3 ± 0.13, KO: 2.1 ± 0.28; t(35)=-2.7, p=0.01).
evidence: This quantifies the intensity of activity during waking.

claim: Cortical temperature was not significantly increased in Cirbp KO mice during the dark phase despite increased locomotor activity.
source: Note that cortical temperature was also not significantly increased in Cirbp KO mice during the dark phase (cortical temperature: WT: 35.9 ± 0.1, KO: 36.1 ± 0.1, t-test, t(10)=1.3, p=0.24) despite increased locomotor activity at this time of the day, again underscoring its minimal contribution to cortical temperature.
evidence: This finding reinforces that locomotor activity has minimal impact on cortical temperature.

claim: Cirbp KO mice did not spend more time in theta-dominated waking during the dark phase of baseline despite their increased locomotor activity.
source: Despite their increased locomotor activity, Cirbp KO mice did not spend more time in theta-dominated waking during the dark phase of baseline (see Table 2, t(31)=-1.22, p=0.23).
evidence: This shows that the waking sub-state distribution is not altered at baseline.

claim: In Cirbp KO mice, slow and fast gamma power were both reduced during theta-dominated waking.
source: In Cirbp KO mice, slow [32–45 Hz] and fast [55–80 Hz] gamma power were both reduced during theta-dominated waking (Figure 6-B), and this reduction was observed throughout the experiment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; and see time course in Figure 6—figure supplement 2), indicating that these spectral differences are robust across different lighting conditions, circadian time and throughout the sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is a primary finding about EEG spectral changes in KO mice.

claim: EEG spectral composition during 'quiet' waking was remarkably similar between Cirbp KO and WT mice.
source: In contrast, EEG spectral composition during 'quiet' waking (i.e. not theta-dominated waking), was remarkably similar between the two genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This shows that the EEG changes are specific to theta-dominated waking.

claim: Theta-peak frequency in theta-dominated waking in baseline was increased in Cirbp KO mice by +0.15 Hz, although the significance threshold was not met.
source: Indeed, theta-peak frequency in this sub-state in baseline was increased in KO mice (+0.15 Hz), although the significance threshold was not met (t(35)=2.0, p=0.0506).
evidence: This is a trend-level finding about theta frequency.

claim: During REM sleep, theta-peak frequency was not affected by CIRBP genotype.
source: During REM sleep, the other sleep-wake state characterized by distinct theta oscillations, theta-peak frequency was not affected (WT: 7.43 ± 0.06; KO: 7.56 ± 0.05, t(35)=1.7, p=0.10).
evidence: This shows that the theta frequency effect is specific to waking.

claim: Mean locomotor activity during the dark phase predicted the mean theta-peak frequency during theta-dominated waking at the same time of day when WT and KO mice were combined.
source: In accordance with this observation, mean log2-transformed locomotor activity in each mouse during the dark phase predicted the mean theta-peak frequency during theta-dominated waking at the same time of day (WT and KO combined; R2 = 0.52, p<0.0001), although this relationship remained significant only in KO mice when assessing the two genotypes separately (Figure 6-C).
evidence: This shows a correlation between activity and theta frequency.

claim: The correlation between locomotor activity and theta-peak frequency remained significant only in KO mice when assessing the two genotypes separately.
source: In accordance with this observation, mean log2-transformed locomotor activity in each mouse during the dark phase predicted the mean theta-peak frequency during theta-dominated waking at the same time of day (WT and KO combined; R2 = 0.52, p<0.0001), although this relationship remained significant only in KO mice when assessing the two genotypes separately (Figure 6-C).
evidence: This shows a genotype-specific relationship.

claim: In the dark phase, the correlation between locomotor activity and theta-peak frequency was significant in all but one mouse.
source: In the dark phase, this correlation was significant in all but one mouse (a KO), and both the slope and the predictive power of this correlation did not significantly differ between genotypes (slope: WT: 0.15 ± 0.01, KO: 0.14 ± 0.01, t(31)=0.37, p=0.72; R2: WT: 0.81 ± 0.03; KO: 0.79 ± 0.04, t-test on the Fisher Z-transformed R2-values: t(31)=-0.49, p=0.62).
evidence: This shows the robustness of the activity-theta frequency relationship within individuals.

claim: Genotype differences in total waking and theta-dominated waking became significant during the dark phases of both recovery days, with Cirbp KO mice spending more time in both than WT mice.
source: Moreover, genotype differences in total waking and theta-dominated waking, became significant during the dark phases of both recovery days, with Cirbp KO mice spending more time in both than WT mice (Figure 6-A; see post-hoc tests indicated by red line), as if sleep deprivation amplified these non-significant genotype differences during baseline (three-way RM ANOVA on hourly values: factor genotype x time x sleep deprivation: total waking: F(41,1271) = 1.4, p=0.04; theta-dominated waking: F(41,1271) = 1.4, p=0.056; but not for locomotor activity F(41,1271) = 1.0, p=0.48).
evidence: This shows that sleep deprivation amplifies genotype differences in waking.

claim: The non-significant increase in theta-peak frequency in Cirbp KO mice during the baseline dark phases became significant during recovery.
source: Similarly, the non-significant increase in theta-peak frequency in Cirbp KO mice during the baseline dark phases became significant during recovery (recovery 1: WT: 8.1 ± 0.05, KO: 8.4 ± 0.07, t(35)=2.7, p=0.01; recovery 2: WT: 8.2 ± 0.05, KO: 8.5 ± 0.08, t(35)=2.6, p=0.01).
evidence: This shows that sleep deprivation amplifies the theta frequency phenotype.

claim: The non-significant genotype difference in slope between theta-peak frequency and locomotor activity during baseline became significant after sleep deprivation.
source: Furthermore, the non-significant genotype difference in slope between theta-peak frequency and locomotor activity during baseline (Figure 6-C), became significant after sleep deprivation (ANCOVA, F(1,29)=5.8, p=0.02), providing further evidence that baseline genotype differences became more pronounced after challenging the sleep homeostat.
evidence: This shows that sleep deprivation reveals latent genotype differences.

claim: The sleep-wake distribution drives cortical temperature changes in the mouse.
source: In this study, we showed that, like in other rodents, the sleep-wake distribution drives cortical temperature changes in the mouse.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study stated in the Discussion.

claim: It is likely that the sleep-wake driven changes in brain temperature drive Cirbp expression.
source: Because of the well-established link between temperature and CIRBP levels, it is likely that also the sleep-wake driven changes in brain temperature drive Cirbp expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge and the study's findings.

claim: Cirbp KO mice were more active during the dark phase, and EEG during theta-dominated waking was characterized by a reduction of gamma activity and faster theta oscillations.
source: Unexpectedly, Cirbp KO mice were more active during the dark phase, and EEG during theta-dominated waking was characterized by a reduction of gamma activity and faster theta oscillations.
evidence: This summarizes unexpected findings from the study.

claim: In humans, 'masking' effects of rest-activity and sleep-wake cycles contributed between 30% and 50% to the amplitude of the circadian body temperature rhythm.
source: The contribution of sleep-wake state to the daily dynamics in body temperature is further supported by forced desynchrony studies, such as (Dijk and Czeisler, 1995), estimating that 'masking' effects of rest-activity and sleep-wake cycles contributed between 30% and 50% to the amplitude of the circadian body temperature rhythm (Hiddinga et al., 1997; Dijk et al., 2000).
evidence: This cites quantitative findings from human studies.

claim: In rats, a circadian and rest-activity component contribute to the circadian fluctuations in body temperature.
source: Not only in humans but also in smaller mammals like rats, a circadian and rest-activity component contribute to the circadian fluctuations in body temperature (Cambras et al., 2007).
evidence: This cites evidence from rat studies.

claim: 80% of the variance in brain temperature in rodents can be explained by the sleep-wake distribution.
source: In contrast to body temperature, brain temperature in rodents is much more determined by sleep-wake state: 80% of its variance can be explained by the sleep-wake distribution (Franken et al., 1992 and this study).
evidence: This cites a previous study and confirms it with the current study's findings.

claim: Sleep-wake-driven changes in brain temperature are still present in arrhythmic animals.
source: Likewise, the sleep-wake-driven changes in brain temperature are still present in arrhythmic animals (Edgar et al., 1993; Baker et al., 2005), pointing to a more important sleep-wake dependency of brain temperature compared to body temperature.
evidence: This cites studies showing that circadian rhythms are not necessary for sleep-wake effects on brain temperature.

claim: Waking with higher locomotor activity was associated with higher cortical temperature.
source: Our study assessed the contribution of locomotor activity and found that waking with higher locomotor activity was associated with higher cortical temperature.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The contribution of locomotor activity to the daily changes in cortical temperature was modest and explained only 2% more of the variance compared to waking alone.
source: Although significant, the contribution of locomotor activity to the daily changes in cortical temperature was modest and explained only 2% more of the variance compared to waking alone.
evidence: This quantifies the modest contribution of locomotor activity.

claim: Rats using a running wheel can increase their brain temperature by 2°C within 30 min.
source: It is important to consider that the influence of locomotor activity on cortical temperature is likely affected by the type of activity; for example, rats using a running wheel can increase their brain temperature by 2°C within 30 min (Fuller et al., 1998).
evidence: This cites evidence that intense exercise can have large effects on brain temperature.

claim: Exercise in humans leads to an increase in proxies of brain temperature.
source: In addition, exercise in humans leads to an increase in (proxies of) brain temperature (Nybo et al., 2002).
evidence: This cites evidence from human studies.

claim: Running speed correlates positively with hippocampal theta-peak frequency.
source: Because running speed correlates positively with hippocampal theta-peak frequency (Jeewajee et al., 2008), and our measured theta activity is mainly of hippocampal origin (Buzsáki, 2006), we indeed can relate this increase in speed of theta oscillations to increased locomotor activity in KO mice.
evidence: This cites established knowledge about the relationship between speed and theta frequency.

claim: Measured theta activity in this study is mainly of hippocampal origin.
source: Because running speed correlates positively with hippocampal theta-peak frequency (Jeewajee et al., 2008), and our measured theta activity is mainly of hippocampal origin (Buzsáki, 2006), we indeed can relate this increase in speed of theta oscillations to increased locomotor activity in KO mice.
evidence: This cites knowledge about the source of theta oscillations.

claim: Some studies have found that increased speed of movement and gamma power are related.
source: Some studies have found that increased speed of movement and gamma power are related (Furth et al., 2017; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Vinck et al., 2015), whereas others found that this association is only present in higher gamma frequencies [>60 Hz] (Zheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites conflicting evidence from the literature about gamma power and movement.

claim: There is a clear increase in high gamma power specifically during the sleep deprivation.
source: However, there is a clear increase in high gamma power specifically during the sleep deprivation (see Figure 6—figure supplement 2), as noted previously (Vassalli and Franken, 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study that confirms a previous observation.

claim: Gamma oscillations are associated with a variety of cognitive processes.
source: Interestingly, gamma oscillations are associated with a variety of cognitive processes (reviewed in Bosman et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites a review about the functional significance of gamma oscillations.

claim: Mice with abnormal interneurons are impaired at the behavioral level and have a reduction in task-evoked gamma power in their EEG.
source: For example, mice with abnormal interneurons are impaired at the behavioral level (e.g. lack of cognitive flexibility) and have a reduction in task-evoked gamma power in their EEG.
evidence: This cites an example linking gamma power to cognitive function.

claim: Pharmacological stimulation of inhibitory GABA-neurons augmented power in the gamma band and rescued the behavioral phenotype of mutants with abnormal interneurons.
source: Pharmacological stimulation of inhibitory GABA-neurons augmented power in the gamma band and rescued the behavioral phenotype of the mutants (Cho et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites evidence that manipulating gamma power can affect behavior.

claim: In the hippocampus, gamma-theta coupling has been suggested to aid processes underlying memory.
source: In the hippocampus, gamma-theta coupling, that is the occurrence of gamma oscillations at a specific phase of the theta oscillation, has been suggested to aid processes underlying memory (for review see Colgin, 2015).
evidence: This cites a review about the functional significance of gamma-theta coupling.

claim: Sleep deprivation amplified genotypic differences in several wake-related phenotypes in Cirbp KO mice.
source: Our data indicates that sleep deprivation has a comparable effect on a number of wake-related phenotypes in Cirbp KO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that several phenotypes became significant after sleep deprivation.

claim: Nr1d1 contributes to several aspects of sleep homeostasis.
source: We recently established that Nr1d1 also contributes to several aspects of sleep homeostasis: Nr1d1 KO mice accumulate NREM sleep need at a slower rate and have reduced efficiency of REM-sleep recovery in the first hours after sleep deprivation (Mang et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites the authors' previous work on Nr1d1 and sleep homeostasis.

claim: Nr1d1 KO mice accumulate NREM sleep need at a slower rate.
source: We recently established that Nr1d1 also contributes to several aspects of sleep homeostasis: Nr1d1 KO mice accumulate NREM sleep need at a slower rate and have reduced efficiency of REM-sleep recovery in the first hours after sleep deprivation (Mang et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites a specific finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Nr1d1 KO mice have reduced efficiency of REM-sleep recovery in the first hours after sleep deprivation.
source: We recently established that Nr1d1 also contributes to several aspects of sleep homeostasis: Nr1d1 KO mice accumulate NREM sleep need at a slower rate and have reduced efficiency of REM-sleep recovery in the first hours after sleep deprivation (Mang et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites a specific finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: The effect of sleep deprivation on clock-gene expression can be modulated by CIRBP directly, or indirectly through the effects of CIRBP on transcriptional clock-gene regulators.
source: Importantly, the effect of sleep deprivation on clock-gene expression can be modulated by CIRBP directly, or indirectly through the effects of CIRBP on transcriptional clock-gene regulators that subsequently affect the expression of downstream clock genes.
evidence: This proposes two possible mechanisms for CIRBP's effects.

claim: Npas2 KO mice showed a reduced increase in Per2 expression in the forebrain after sleep deprivation.
source: For example, Npas2 KO mice showed a reduced increase in Per2 expression in the forebrain after sleep deprivation (Franken et al., 2006), while Cry1,2 double-KO mice display a larger increase in Per2 expression after sleep deprivation (Wisor et al., 2008).
evidence: This cites evidence that clock gene mutations affect Per2 responses to sleep deprivation.

claim: Cry1,2 double-KO mice display a larger increase in Per2 expression after sleep deprivation.
source: For example, Npas2 KO mice showed a reduced increase in Per2 expression in the forebrain after sleep deprivation (Franken et al., 2006), while Cry1,2 double-KO mice display a larger increase in Per2 expression after sleep deprivation (Wisor et al., 2008).
evidence: This cites evidence that clock gene mutations affect Per2 responses to sleep deprivation.

claim: Mutations in clock genes incurred a loss in REM-sleep recovery in Clock mutant mice.
source: This is supported by studies showing that mutations in clock genes incurred a loss in REM-sleep recovery (i.e. Clock [Naylor et al., 2000]), or impacted the initial efficiency of REM-sleep recovery (i.e. Dbp [Franken et al., 2000], Per3 [Hasan et al., 2011], and Nr1d1 [Mang et al., 2016]).
evidence: This cites evidence linking clock genes to REM sleep homeostasis.

claim: Mutations in Dbp, Per3, and Nr1d1 impacted the initial efficiency of REM-sleep recovery.
source: This is supported by studies showing that mutations in clock genes incurred a loss in REM-sleep recovery (i.e. Clock [Naylor et al., 2000]), or impacted the initial efficiency of REM-sleep recovery (i.e. Dbp [Franken et al., 2000], Per3 [Hasan et al., 2011], and Nr1d1 [Mang et al., 2016]).
evidence: This cites evidence linking clock genes to REM sleep homeostasis.

claim: RBM3 is another cold-inducible transcript which is closely related to CIRBP.
source: Rbm3, another cold-inducible transcript which is closely related to CIRBP, translates temperature information into high amplitude clock-gene expression in vitro (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This states a known relationship between RBM3 and CIRBP.

claim: RBM3 translates temperature information into high amplitude clock-gene expression in vitro.
source: Rbm3, another cold-inducible transcript which is closely related to CIRBP, translates temperature information into high amplitude clock-gene expression in vitro (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This cites in vitro evidence for RBM3's role in clock gene regulation.

claim: Cortical expression of Rbm3 is sleep-wake driven.
source: Like Cirbp, its cortical expression is sleep-wake driven (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This cites evidence that RBM3 expression is regulated by sleep-wake state.

claim: Heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1) is a member of the heat shock pathway.
source: Heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1) is a member of the heat shock pathway and in vitro studies have shown that it transfers temperature information to the circadian clock by initiating Per2 transcription through binding to Per2's upstream heat shock elements (Tamaru et al., 2011).
evidence: This states a known fact about Hsf1.

claim: Hsf1 transfers temperature information to the circadian clock by initiating Per2 transcription through binding to Per2's upstream heat shock elements.
source: Heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1) is a member of the heat shock pathway and in vitro studies have shown that it transfers temperature information to the circadian clock by initiating Per2 transcription through binding to Per2's upstream heat shock elements (Tamaru et al., 2011).
evidence: This cites in vitro evidence for Hsf1's mechanism of action.

claim: Under undisturbed conditions, both Hsf1 mRNA and protein levels are constitutively expressed.
source: Under undisturbed conditions, both Hsf1 mRNA and protein levels are constitutively expressed, but the protein exhibits daily re-localization during the dark phase to the nucleus where it acts as a transcription factor (Reinke et al., 2008).
evidence: This cites evidence about Hsf1 expression and localization patterns.

claim: HSF1 protein exhibits daily re-localization during the dark phase to the nucleus where it acts as a transcription factor.
source: Under undisturbed conditions, both Hsf1 mRNA and protein levels are constitutively expressed, but the protein exhibits daily re-localization during the dark phase to the nucleus where it acts as a transcription factor (Reinke et al., 2008).
evidence: This cites evidence about Hsf1 protein dynamics.

claim: CIRBP binds to the 3'UTR of Hsf1 transcript.
source: Interestingly, CIRBP binds to the 3'UTR of Hsf1 transcript (Morf et al., 2012, see supplementary data therein), although it is unclear if this affects the transcriptional activity of HSF1.
evidence: This cites evidence for a molecular interaction between CIRBP and Hsf1.

claim: Sleep deprivation induced a significant increase in Hsf1 in Cirbp KO mice only.
source: We found that sleep deprivation induced a significant increase in Hsf1 in KO mice only, which is congruent with the observation that the expression of two other transcripts of the heat shock pathway, Hsp90b1 and Hspa5, were significantly amplified in KO mice after sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: Per2 can act as a sensor of stress, light, and temperature.
source: This has been well documented for Per2 which can act as a sensor of stress, light, and temperature (Franken, 2013; Schibler et al., 2015), which is especially relevant in sleep deprivation studies.
evidence: This cites evidence that Per2 responds to multiple stimuli.

claim: Oxygen consumption varies with sleep-wake state.
source: Another example is oxygen consumption which varies with sleep-wake state (Jung et al., 2011).
evidence: This cites evidence for metabolic changes across sleep-wake states.

claim: Changes in oxygen levels can modulate the expression of clock genes through HIF1α.
source: Changes in oxygen levels can modulate the expression of clock genes through HIF1α (Adamovich et al., 2017).
evidence: This cites evidence for an oxygen-dependent pathway affecting clock genes.

claim: During sleep deprivation, corticosterone levels increase, which subsequently amplifies the expression of some, but not all, clock genes.
source: Moreover, during sleep deprivation, corticosterone levels increase, which subsequently amplifies the expression of some, but not all, clock genes (Mongrain et al., 2010).
evidence: This cites evidence for a stress hormone pathway affecting clock genes during sleep deprivation.

claim: The current study could not corroborate the hepatic increase in heat shock transcripts (Hsf1, Hsp90b1 and Hspa5) and in Per2 after sleep deprivation as reported in other studies.
source: We could not corroborate the hepatic increase in heat shock transcripts (Hsf1, Hsp90b1 and Hspa5) and in Per2 after sleep deprivation as reported in other studies (Diessler et al., 2018; Maret et al., 2007), whereas we did confirm the sleep-deprivation-induced changes in Cirbp, Rbm3-short, Dbp and Nr1d1.
evidence: This acknowledges a discrepancy between the current study and previous work.

claim: The current study confirmed the sleep-deprivation-induced changes in Cirbp, Rbm3-short, Dbp and Nr1d1 in the liver.
source: We could not corroborate the hepatic increase in heat shock transcripts (Hsf1, Hsp90b1 and Hspa5) and in Per2 after sleep deprivation as reported in other studies (Diessler et al., 2018; Maret et al., 2007), whereas we did confirm the sleep-deprivation-induced changes in Cirbp, Rbm3-short, Dbp and Nr1d1.
evidence: This states which findings were replicated from previous studies.

claim: Unpublished observations indicate an increased circadian amplitude of CLOCK:ARNTL target genes in the liver of Cirbp KO mice.
source: Unpublished observations on the circadian dynamics of the expression of CLOCK:ARNTL target genes in the liver, such as Nr1d1 and Dbp, indicate an increased circadian amplitude in Cirbp KO mice; that is the opposite phenotype from that observed in vitro (mentioned in Schibler et al., 2015).
evidence: This mentions unpublished data that contradicts in vitro findings.

claim: Disturbance of clock-gene expression through genetic manipulations in mice or shift work in humans can lead to the development of metabolic disorders.
source: This is supported by the observation that disturbance of clock-gene expression, through for example genetic manipulations in mice or shift work in humans, can lead to the development of metabolic disorders (Rudic et al., 2004) (Karlsson et al., 2001).
evidence: This cites evidence linking circadian disruption to metabolic disease.

claim: Sleeping too little or of poor quality can induce disturbed metabolic state both in rats and humans.
source: Not only sleeping at the wrong time, but also sleeping too little or of poor quality can induce disturbed metabolic state both in rats (Barf et al., 2010) and humans (Copinschi et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites evidence linking sleep loss to metabolic dysfunction.

claim: Sleep loss affects clock-gene expression.
source: Because sleep loss affects clock-gene expression (Franken, 2013), we propose that this could represent a common pathway through which both sleep and circadian disturbances lead to metabolic pathologies.
evidence: This cites evidence and proposes a mechanistic link.

claim: Changes in clock-gene expression could represent a common pathway through which both sleep and circadian disturbances lead to metabolic pathologies.
source: Because sleep loss affects clock-gene expression (Franken, 2013), we propose that this could represent a common pathway through which both sleep and circadian disturbances lead to metabolic pathologies.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Nr1d1 is important for healthy metabolic functioning.
source: Genetic (Delezie et al., 2012) and pharmacological (Solt et al., 2012) studies have shown that this transcriptional repressor is important for healthy metabolic functioning.
evidence: This cites evidence for Nr1d1's role in metabolism.
